content.thinking:
I need to be careful not to invent any numbers myself, relying only on placeholder figures for citations. The core narrative is that account pages show elevated p99 latency for a subset of shoppers without a corresponding rise in errors, so I'm working out which sources to cite to support that specific chain of evidence.

The root cause ties back to the feature flag enabling a quadratic computation path — a reading I should flag as unverified since nothing directly confirms it ran that way, though the revert test does corroborate the flag as the actual cause. I'm also ruling out deployments and config changes since none occurred, isolating the flag as the sole change, while noting a slight timestamp discrepancy between when the flag event was logged and when the latency onset actually began.

Now I'm laying out the incident timeline: duration, p99 latency figures before/during/peak impact, flat error rates, the detection gap between onset and alert, and the revert/mitigation timing which coincided exactly with recovery. I'm also noting contributing factors like the absence of pre-enable performance testing for flag toggles, which feeds into a follow-up action item.

I'm settling on two numbered action items — AI-3 for staged flag rollout with a latency guard, and AI-4 for testing the quadratic latency behavior on the lifetime path — and deciding to keep the writeup factual rather than speculating on confirmation of the root cause. I'm also noting what went well: the fast revert after the alert fired, and the investigator's work connecting the pieces.

We got lucky that errors stayed flat and only long-history shoppers were hit, but the fix itself is still just an unmerged draft PR with the flag left off — that's the real gap to flag. I'll mention the pre-existing ClientDisconnected log noise briefly as an unrelated assumption, then write this up.

action_items.item: Add a progressive rollout step with a p99 latency check for monthly-spend-feature and similar flags, so a flag that raises p99 is rolled back automatically or blocked from reaching full traffic.

Add a long-history latency test for the lifetime figure, spend_summary.average_spend_per_item, which Code-Fix noted also recomputes a running sum quadratically, and fix it if the test shows slow behaviour.

causal_chain.step: Users saw slow account pages, not failed ones. p99 latency went from {series_before} before the onset to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at worst, so the slowest requests were the ones affected. The error rate did not rise: {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before, peaking at {errors_at_worst}. The HighLatency alert fired because p99 stayed above its threshold.

The slowdown started when the feature flag monthly-spend-feature began serving ON. Flag evaluations were 3 of 200 on at 15:50 and all on from 15:51, matching the onset at {began}. Before that the flag was off in the logs. The change record shows the flag toggle as {P1.1}.

The flag is the only change seen. Argus read {T9.2} production deploys or releases in the 24 hours before the onset, and the flag provider showed one recent flag change. Reverting the flag took latency back to normal, which confirms it as the trigger.

Only the slowest requests slowed, not the median or p95. Code-Fix's reading of the source is that the flag-gated typical-spend figure finds the lower-middle price by removing the minimum from the list about n/2 times, with each removal scanning the whole list. Work is then quadratic in the length of the shopper's history. Short histories cost almost nothing, while the few long ones take seconds. This is a static reading that nothing ran, so it is unverified.

The same reading explains why errors did not rise. The other flag-related summary paths would raise on a shopper with no purchases and would have raised the error rate. The typical-spend path fails only where the existing lifetime path already failed, so it adds latency but no errors. This is also unverified, and the record does not show why the slow path was released without a long-history check.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from a small share to fully on within the logged window. No latency guard or automatic rollback tied to p99 was seen in the record, so the slow path reached all traffic until the paging alert fired and Argus reverted it.

No test or check was seen that exercises the spend-figure code with very long purchase histories, so the quadratic cost was not caught before the flag was enabled. The lifetime path, which is the default, has the same shape of cost according to the code reading.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, a small share of shoppers on io-shop saw very slow account pages. The slowest requests went from about {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and {series_at_worst} at worst on the latency measure that paged. Typical requests were not slowed, and the share of failed requests did not rise: {errors_while_broken} while broken against {errors_before} before. The slowdown began when the feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on. Argus reverted the flag and latency returned to normal. A draft pull request with a proposed code fix has been opened but not yet merged.

got_lucky: The slow path added latency but no errors, and only shoppers with long histories were affected. The harm was limited to the slowest requests.
The incident coincided with a single flag change and no deploys, so the trigger was easy to isolate.
went_well: Argus tied the onset to the flag change and reverted the flag within moments of forming its candidate, and the metrics were back to normal at {back_to_normal}.
The revert was checked against the service afterwards and judged confirmed rather than assumed.
Code-Fix proposed a draft pull request with a regression test for the long-history case.
went_wrong: The paging rule waits {rule_waits} before firing, so the alert came well after the onset at {began}. During that time users with long histories saw slow pages.
The proposed fix is still an unmerged draft, so the flag cannot yet be safely turned back on.

input.root_cause: Switching on the feature flag monthly-spend-feature sent requests down the "typical purchase" code path. Code-Fix's reading of the source, which nothing ran and so is unverified, is that this path finds the lower-middle price by repeatedly removing the minimum from the shopper's purchase list. That work grows quadratically with history length, so the few shoppers with long histories became very slow. Reverting the flag removed the slowdown, which confirms the flag as the trigger. The quadratic cost is only a reading of the code.
input.symptom: Account pages were very slow for some shoppers
